title: 10. Exercises: Lists & Tuples Masterclass (Part 2)
objectives: Solve the Lists & Tuples Masterclass exercises without looking at the lesson
Test edge cases and explain your approach

sections.title: Advanced Tuple Patterns — CODING CHALLENGES — Chapter 23
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
Implement a "persistent linked list" using tuples:
cons(head, tail) → (head, tail)  — like Lisp/Haskell
car(lst) → head element
cdr(lst) → rest of list
list_to_plist(*items) → persistent list
plist_to_list(plist)  → regular list
length(plist)         → count elements (recursively)
map_plist(func, plist) → apply func to each element
filter_plist(pred, plist) → keep matching elements
reduce_plist(func, plist, init) → fold
reverse_plist(plist)  → reversed persistent list

CHALLENGE 2:
Build a "functional state machine" using tuples:
State = (state_name: str, data: tuple, history: tuple)
transition(state, event, handlers_dict) → new State
handlers_dict = {
    ("idle","start"):    lambda s: s._replace(state_name="running"),
    ("running","pause"): lambda s: s._replace(state_name="paused"),
}
All transitions create new State tuples.
history grows with each transition.
rollback(state, n) → state n transitions ago.
replay(initial_state, events) → sequence of all states.

CHALLENGE 3:
Implement "tuple-based vector math" for a 3D physics engine:
Vector = tuple of (x, y, z)
Operations (all return tuples):
add, subtract, scale, dot, cross, normalize, magnitude
reflect(v, normal), refract(v, normal, ior)
lerp(v1, v2, t)    → linear interpolation
Matrix3x3 = tuple of 3 Vector tuples
mat_mul(m1, m2), mat_vec_mul(m, v), determinant(m)
inverse(m), transpose(m)
All pure functions, no mutation.

CHALLENGE 4:
Create a "time-travel debugger" using immutable tuple states:
Debugger(initial_state: tuple)
.step(transformation_func) → apply func, save new state
.undo(n=1)     → go back n steps
.redo(n=1)     → go forward n steps
.branch(name)  → create named branch at current point
.merge(branch_name, merge_func) → merge branch back
.diff(step1, step2) → what changed between steps
.visualize()   → ASCII timeline of states and branches

CHALLENGE 5:
Build a "declarative query system" using tuple patterns:
Query language as tuples:
query = (
    ("SELECT", "name", "salary"),
    ("FROM",   employees_tuple),
    ("WHERE",  ("dept", "==", "Engineering")),
    ("AND",    ("salary", ">", 80000)),
    ("ORDER",  "salary", "DESC"),
    ("LIMIT",  10),
)
parse_query(query) → executable query plan
execute_query(plan, data) → result tuple
All results returned as tuples of tuples.

CHALLENGE 6:
Implement an "event sourcing" system with tuples:
Events stored as immutable tuples: (event_type, payload, timestamp, version)
EventStore():
.append(event_type, **payload) → create + store event
.replay(entity_id) → reconstruct current state from all events
.snapshot(entity_id) → save current state tuple for fast replay
.project(event_type) → list of all events of that type
.time_travel(entity_id, timestamp) → state at that moment
.undo_last(entity_id) → state without last event
All state is pure tuples — no mutation anywhere.

CHALLENGE 7:
Build a "pattern matching engine" for tuples:
match(data, pattern) → True/False + captured groups
Patterns:
- Exact: (1, 2, 3) → matches only (1,2,3)
- Wildcard: (_, _, 3) → matches any 2 items then 3
- Type: (int, str, _) → matches (int, str, anything)
- Star: (1, *rest) → matches 1 followed by anything
- Guard: (x,) if x > 0 → matches single positive int
- Nested: ((a, b), c) → matches nested tuples
match_all(data, *patterns) → list of matching patterns
Used for: command parsing, protocol handling, rule engines.
```
